title: Predict the Winner
spaceBreakdown:
- vector<int> dp: n entries → O(n)
- recursion: none (iterative)
- not counted: input nums
approach: Track the score difference (current player − opponent) rather than individual scores. For subarray [i..j], the current player picks an end, then the opponent plays optimally on the remainder: diff = max(nums[i] − diff(i+1,j), nums[j] − diff(i,j−1)). Since length-L subproblems depend only on length-(L−1) subproblems, a single 1D array updated left-to-right by increasing length suffices. Player 1 wins iff the difference for the full array is ≥ 0.
hints: With both players playing optimally, what single quantity about any remaining contiguous subarray fully determines the outcome, instead of tracking each player's score separately?

1D dynamic programming on intervals: dp[i] stores the best score difference (current player minus opponent) for the subarray of the current length starting at index i. For [1,5,233,7], the length-2 window [5,233] yields dp = max(5−233, 233−5) = 228.

```
dp[i] = nums[i]  for all i  (length 1)
for len = 2 to n:
    for i = 0 to n - len:
        j = i + len - 1
        dp[i] = max(nums[i] - dp[i+1], nums[j] - dp[i])
return dp[0] >= 0
```

**Single element** - only one number exists, Player 1 takes it immediately
`Input: [0]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: using `dp[0] > 0` instead of `dp[0] >= 0` → returns false

**Tie** - both players end with equal scores
`Input: [5,5]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: using `>` instead of `>=` in the final return → returns false

**Greedy fails** - always picking the larger end is suboptimal
`Input: [1,5,233,7]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: greedy strategy (pick max of both ends each turn) → P1 picks 7, P2 picks 233, P1 picks 5, P2 picks 1; P1=12 < P2=234 → returns false

**Off-by-one loop bound** - skipping the last subarray of each length
`Input: [1,5,2]` → `Expected: false`
⚠️ Bug: writing `i < n - len` instead of `i <= n - len` → length-2 loop only processes i=0, length-3 loop never runs, dp[0]=4 ≥ 0 → returns true

followUps.q: What if the array length is up to 10^5?
followUps.a: When n is even, Player 1 can always force at least a tie by choosing to collect all even-indexed or all odd-indexed elements (whichever sum is larger), so return true in O(n). When n is odd, the general case still requires O(n²) interval DP, so additional constraints would be needed.

followUps.q: What if there are three players instead of two?
followUps.a: The zero-sum assumption breaks: maximizing your score is no longer equivalent to minimizing total opponent score. The state must track all three players' scores, making the DP state O(n² × S²) where S is the total sum. The 1D space optimization no longer applies because dependencies span multiple opponent score dimensions.

followUps.q: What if elements are appended to the right one at a time and you must answer after each append?
followUps.a: Each new element extends every interval ending at the new right boundary. Recomputing the full DP from scratch gives O(n²) per query and O(n³) total. A more efficient approach reuses prior length computations but still requires O(n) work per append in the worst case, yielding O(n²) total.
